definition: Petroleum is a liquid fossil fuel: decayed organic matter buried under heat and pressure over geologic time converts into a mixture of hydrocarbons, some of which are liquid at normal temperature and pressure.
core_idea: "Petroleum" is a generic term covering crude oil as extracted plus every product later refined from it; "crude oil" specifically means the unrefined liquid as it comes out of the ground.
key_points: Fossil-fuel hydrocarbon mixtures can be gas, liquid, or solid depending on composition.
Crude oil is the raw, undistilled extracted liquid; distillation splits it into named products (gasoline, heating oil, etc.).

Petroleum's high energy density per unit volume makes it a favored transportation fuel versus gaseous hydrocarbons (e.g., propane) and easier to handle in an engine than solid hydrocarbons (e.g., coal).
caveats: Using "petroleum" and "crude oil" interchangeably — the author distinguishes crude oil (unrefined) from petroleum (the whole crude-plus-refined-products family).
